title: How do you find the middle element of a linked list (slow/fast pointer)?
shortTitle: Find middle element of a linked list — slow/fast pointer

s1_definition.profdef: The tortoise-and-hare algorithm: two pointers start at head. `slow` moves 1 step, `fast` moves 2 steps. When `fast` reaches the end, `slow` is at the middle. For even-length: slow points to the second of the two middle elements. Time: O(n). Space: O(1). No need to know the size beforehand.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The tortoise-and-hare algorithm: two pointers start at head. `slow` moves 1 step, `fast` moves 2 steps. When `fast` reaches the end, `slow` is at the middle. For even-length: slow points to the second of the two middle elements. Time: O(n). Space: O(1). No need to know the size beforehand.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A queue of customers. One clerk (slow) processes 1 customer at a time. Another clerk (fast) processes 2 at a time. When the fast clerk finishes the entire queue, the slow clerk is exactly at the middle customer — that's your VIP customer for priority service.

**One line to remember:** slow = slow.next, fast = fast.next.next. When fast reaches end, slow is at middle. O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.s2_technical:
Finding the middle of a singly linked list in one pass uses the slow/fast pointer (tortoise and hare) technique. A slow pointer advances one node at a time while a fast pointer advances two; when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is at the middle. This is O(n) time and O(1) extra space, with no need to first count the length.

The key invariant: when fast has moved 2k steps, slow has moved k steps, so slow is always at half the distance fast has travelled. For an even-length list you choose a convention — stopping when `fast != null && fast.next != null` lands slow on the second of the two middle nodes. Streams are not ideal here because linked traversal is inherently sequential with pointer state.

A banking example: a transaction history is held as a linked list and an auditor wants the median-position entry quickly without buffering the whole list into another structure. The slow/fast scan finds it in a single traversal. Senior nuance: slow/fast is the same core trick used for cycle detection (Floyd's algorithm) and for finding the k-th node from the end.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — A transaction history held as a singly linked list needed its middle entry for a median-position audit, but counting the length then re-traversing was two passes over a long list. Fix: the slow/fast pointer technique finds the middle in a single O(n) pass using O(1) extra memory.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: list 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40 -> 50.

**Step 2.** slow and fast both start at node 10.

**Step 3.** Iteration 1: slow moves to 20, fast moves to 30.

**Step 4.** Iteration 2: slow moves to 30, fast moves to 50; fast.next is null so the loop stops.

**Step 5.** slow is at 30 — the middle node — returned in a single pass.

```text
INFO: middle = 30
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5

  Step 0: slow=1, fast=1
  Step 1: slow=2, fast=3
  Step 2: slow=3, fast=5
  Step 3: fast.next=null → STOP. slow=3 ← MIDDLE!
```

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Slow/Fast Pointer (Transaction Queue — find middle txn)   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  head ─► T1 ─► T2 ─► T3 ─► T4 ─► T5 ─► null                 │
│         slow+1 per step   │   fast+2 per step              │
│                           ▼                                │
│  iter1: slow=T2 fast=T3                                    │
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Node + traversal (linked list of Txn)                    │
│───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│ class Node { Txn val; Node next; }                       │
│ Node slow = head, fast = head;                           │
│ while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {              │
│     slow = slow.next;        // 1 step                   │
│     fast = fast.next.next;   // 2 steps                  │
│ }                                                        │
│ return slow.val;  // middle transaction                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Parity behaviour (settlement batch)                      │
│───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│ ODD  n=5  [T1 T2 T3 T4 T5] → slow=T3 (true middle)       │
│ EVEN n=4  [T1 T2 T3 T4]    → slow=T3 (2nd of two mids)   │
│ Use case: pick median-position cheque for sample audit   │
│ No need to call size()/count first — single traversal    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The slow/fast pointer (tortoise-and-hare) finds the middle of a linked list in one pass. slow advances 1 node, fast advances 2 nodes per iteration. When fast reaches the end (null or null.next), slow is at the middle. For even-length lists, slow points to the second middle element. O(n) time, O(1) space, and you don't need to know the list size beforehand — which is the whole point of this approach.
